blocks.prompt: How Cheese Gets Its Holes
blocks.text: Cheese begins as milk. To turn milk into cheese, the milk is left to get thick and lumpy. The soft lumps are called curds. The watery part left over is called whey. The curds are pressed together to make cheese. Some cheese has round holes in it. These holes are called eyes. The eyes are made by tiny living things called bacteria. As the cheese sits in a warm room, the bacteria make gas. The gas cannot get out, so it makes a bubble. When the cheese is cut open, you can see the bubble as a hole. Cheese can take many days, or even years, to be ready.

blocks.prompt: Why Swiss Cheese Has Holes
blocks.text: People have made cheese for a very long time. Scientists have found bits of cheese on old pots that are more than seven thousand years old. That makes cheese one of the oldest foods that people know how to make. Cheese starts as milk. A cheesemaker adds something that makes the milk split into two parts. The thick, solid part is the curds. The thin, watery part is the whey. The curds are pressed, salted, and left to age. The round holes in Swiss cheese have a special name. They are called eyes. Long ago, people did not know what made them. Now we know the answer is bacteria. These tiny living things feed on the cheese and give off a gas called carbon dioxide. The gas is trapped inside the firm cheese, so it gathers into bubbles. Each bubble slowly pushes the cheese apart and leaves a round hole behind. A warmer room makes bigger eyes. Cheese with no eyes at all has a funny name too. Cheesemakers call it blind.

blocks.prompt: The Holes Are Alive
blocks.text: Cheese is one of the oldest foods humans know how to make. Archaeologists have found the chemical traces of cheese on broken pottery more than seven thousand years old. People almost certainly discovered it by accident, when milk stored in warm conditions curdled into soft lumps and a thin liquid. Those two parts have names. The solid lumps are curds, and the liquid is whey. To make cheese on purpose, a cheesemaker encourages the milk to separate, usually by adding an acid or a substance called rennet. The curds are then cut, drained, salted, and pressed into shape. After that, most cheese is aged, sometimes for years, in cool and steady conditions. The famous holes in Swiss cheese are the work of bacteria. Cheesemakers add helpful bacteria on purpose. As the young cheese rests in a warm room, one kind of bacteria feeds on the acids in the curd and releases carbon dioxide gas. Because the cheese around it is firm, the gas cannot escape. Instead it collects into round pockets that slowly stretch the cheese open. Each pocket becomes a hole, which cheesemakers call an eye. The warmth of the aging room, the type of bacteria, and the length of aging all decide how big the eyes grow. A cheese that comes out with no eyes is described as blind. There is a surprising twist to this story. For years, Swiss eyes were getting smaller, and no one knew why. Researchers eventually discovered that tiny specks of hay dust in the milk had been helping the bubbles to form. As milking machines grew cleaner, the dust disappeared, and so did some of the holes.

blocks.prompt: The Mystery of the Shrinking Holes
blocks.text: Cheese may be one of the first foods that humans learned to manufacture rather than simply gather. Chemists analyzing broken pottery from sites more than seven thousand years old have found the fatty residues of processed milk, evidence that people were separating milk into solids and liquid long before written history. The likeliest origin is an accident. Milk carried in a warm climate curdles on its own, dividing into soft white lumps and a watery liquid. Someone tasted the lumps, found them good, and a craft was born. Those two parts still have their old names. The solid is the curd, and the liquid is the whey. A modern cheesemaker separates them deliberately by adding an acid or an enzyme called rennet, which causes the proteins in milk to clump together. The curds are cut, heated, drained, salted, and pressed, and then most cheeses are aged in cool, controlled conditions where flavor slowly develops. The holes in Swiss cheese, however, are a separate marvel, and for a long time they were a mystery. Cheesemakers deliberately add bacteria to the milk. One species feeds on the lactic acid in the young cheese and burps out carbon dioxide. Because the surrounding cheese is dense and elastic, the gas cannot escape. It pools into round bubbles that gradually push the cheese apart, and each bubble becomes what cheesemakers call an eye. Warmer aging rooms and longer aging produce larger eyes; a wheel that emerges without any is called blind. The strangest chapter came recently. Through the twentieth century, the eyes in Swiss cheese were shrinking, and no one could explain it. In 2015, researchers in Switzerland cracked the case. The bubbles had been forming around microscopic specks of hay dust that fell into open buckets during hand milking. As milking moved to sealed, sanitary machines, the dust vanished, and the holes shrank with it. The famous eyes of Swiss cheese, it turned out, depended on a trace of barnyard dust that nobody had ever noticed.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: A Trick Played on Milk
blocks.text: Cheese is a trick played on milk, and it is one of the oldest tricks in the human kitchen. Milk is mostly water, and the useful parts, its fats and proteins, are suspended invisibly throughout it. Left alone in a warm place, milk sours and separates on its own into soft curds and thin whey. Somewhere more than seven thousand years ago, someone ate those curds instead of throwing them out, and cheesemaking began. We know the date because chemists have identified the fatty residues of processed milk on pottery fragments from Neolithic sites, hard evidence of a craft older than writing. The craft has a clear logic. A cheesemaker wants to capture the solids and drain away the water, and to do it on purpose rather than by luck. The milk is encouraged to separate, usually by adding an acid or an enzyme called rennet, which makes the milk proteins bond together and trap the fat. The result is a mass of curd sitting in a pool of whey. From there the choices multiply: cut the curd fine or leave it coarse, heat it or not, wash it, salt it, press it hard or barely at all, and then age it for weeks or years. Every choice steers the final cheese. The difference between a fresh, squeaky curd and a sharp aged wheel is not a difference of ingredient but a difference of handling and time. The holes in Swiss cheese are a good example of how much is happening invisibly inside a wheel. They are not cut or poked. They are made by living things. Cheesemakers deliberately add bacteria, and one particular species feeds on the lactic acid in the young cheese and releases carbon dioxide as a waste gas. Because the body of the cheese is dense and slightly elastic, the gas has nowhere to go. It collects into round bubbles that slowly stretch the cheese from the inside, and each finished bubble is what a cheesemaker calls an eye. The warmth of the aging room, the strain of bacteria, and the length of aging all shape how large and how many the eyes become. A wheel that comes out solid, with no eyes, has its own name: it is called blind. For most of the twentieth century, though, something strange was happening, and no one could explain it. The eyes in Swiss cheese were slowly shrinking, decade by decade, even though the recipe had not changed. In 2015, researchers at a Swiss agricultural institute finally solved the puzzle, and the answer was almost comic. The bubbles had never formed on nothing. They had been forming around microscopic specks of hay dust that drifted into open buckets during old-fashioned hand milking. The dust gave the gas a place to gather, the same way a scratch in a glass gives a bubble somewhere to start. As dairies switched to sealed, sanitary milking machines, the barnyard dust disappeared from the milk, and the holes shrank right along with it. The most admired feature of the cheese, it turned out, had depended for centuries on a bit of dirt that nobody had ever meant to add. That is the quiet lesson buried in a wedge of Swiss cheese. What looks like a fixed recipe is really a living process, balanced between the cheesemaker's careful choices and a crowd of bacteria, acids, gases, and even stray dust doing their own work in the dark. The eye you see when you cut a slice is the fossil of a bubble, and the bubble is the record of a small, invisible life.
